en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on Garlic 6.
The Training Rule on Attending Upon.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a high official named Ārohanta had gone forth among the monks.
His former wife had also gone forth among the nuns.
At that time, that monk was taking his meal in the presence of that nun.
Then that bhikkhunī, while standing by that bhikkhu as he was eating, attending to him with drinking water and a fan, spoke excessively to him.
Then that bhikkhu rebuked that bhikkhunī:
"Sister, do not act in such a way."
“This is not permitted.
“Previously you did such and such things to me, yet now you do not dare even this much!
Having said this, she struck him on the head with a water-pitcher and dealt him a blow with a fan.
Those bhikkhunīs who were modest … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can a bhikkhunī give a blow to a bhikkhu? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī gave a blow to a bhikkhu?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can a bhikkhunī give a blow to a bhikkhu?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, should the nuns recite this training rule:
‘If any bhikkhunī stands by a bhikkhu while he is eating, offering him water or a fan, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such... "nun" means...
[as before]... nun.
... [as before] ... this is the nun intended in this context. "Of a bhikkhu" means of one who is fully ordained.
"Of one who is eating" means:
of one who is eating any one of the five kinds of cooked food.
"Drink" means:
Any kind of drinking water.
A fan is any kind of handheld fan.
"Should attend upon":
if she stands within arm's reach, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she attends upon one who is ordained, perceiving them as ordained, with either drinking water or a fan, there is an offense of expiation.
If one attends upon a person who is fully ordained while being in doubt [about their status], whether with drinking water or a fan, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one attends upon a person who is fully ordained while perceiving them as not fully ordained, whether with drinking water or a fan, there is an offense of expiation.
If one attends upon them after having stepped outside the reach of hand-contact, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one stands waiting for someone eating solid food, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one stands waiting for one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives as fully ordained someone who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If there is doubt regarding one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is one who is not fully ordained and she perceives them as such, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—
gives it,
causes it to be given,
or commands one who is not fully ordained [to do so].
"In the case of one who is insane,
or in the case of one who is a first-offender.
The sixth training rule is concluded.
